sources.label: Source A
sources.title: Speech at the Opening of the Convention for a Democratic South Africa (CODESA)
sources.author: Nelson Mandela
sources.publication: Convention for a Democratic South Africa, Kempton Park
sources.content:
We meet here today as leaders of political parties, organisations and administrations, representing the broad spectrum of our people. We have come from different political traditions, and we have been divided by a history of conflict and oppression. Yet we are here because we share a common determination to end the system of apartheid and to create a democratic South Africa based on the will of the people.

The road to this Convention has not been easy. It has been marked by pain, suffering and the loss of many lives. But the courage of our people, and the growing recognition among all South Africans that a negotiated settlement is the only way forward, have brought us to this point.

We must not underestimate the difficulties ahead. There are those who will seek to derail the process, who will use violence to oppose the will of the majority. But we must not be deterred. The eyes of the world are upon us, and the hopes of millions of South Africans rest on our ability to reach a just and lasting peace.

We are committed to a unitary, non-racial, non-sexist South Africa. We are committed to a Bill of Rights and to a constitution that enshrines the principles of democracy and human dignity. We are committed to a government that is elected by all the people and that serves all the people.

Let us seize this historic opportunity. Let us negotiate in good faith, and let us build a South Africa that future generations will be proud of. The time for change is now.
sources.context: CODESA was the first formal multi-party negotiation forum in South Africa, bringing together the apartheid government, the ANC, and other political groups. It marked the beginning of the transition from apartheid to democracy. Mandela's speech set the tone for negotiations, emphasising unity, non-racialism, and the need to overcome violence and extremism. The talks were fraught with tension and ultimately collapsed in mid-1992, but they laid the groundwork for the later Multi-Party Negotiating Forum.

sources.label: Source B
sources.title: Voters Queue at a Polling Station in Soweto, 27 April 1994
sources.author: Unknown (Associated Press photographer)
sources.content: The photograph shows a long, winding queue of South Africans of all races, mainly Black, snaking through a dusty street in Soweto, Johannesburg. People are standing patiently, some holding small children, others clutching identity documents and voter registration slips. In the background, a simple polling station is visible, with a sign reading 'VOTE HERE' and the IEC (Independent Electoral Commission) logo. The atmosphere is one of determination and hope, with many people smiling and waving to the camera. A few elderly women are seen in traditional dress, while younger voters wear casual Western clothing. The photo captures the historic nature of the day, as millions of South Africans voted for the first time in a democratic election.
sources.context: The 1994 election was the first fully democratic election in South Africa, held after decades of apartheid and four years of negotiations. The election was marred by political violence, especially in KwaZulu-Natal and the Witwatersrand, and by threats from right-wing groups. Despite this, voter turnout was exceptionally high, with over 19.5 million people casting ballots. The photograph symbolises the peaceful and hopeful participation of ordinary South Africans, particularly the Black majority who had been denied the vote for centuries. The ANC won the election with 62.6% of the vote, and Nelson Mandela was inaugurated as the first democratically elected president on 10 May 1994.

sources.label: Source C
sources.title: From 'Long Walk to Freedom'
sources.author: Nelson Mandela
sources.content:
The election of 27 April 1994 was the culmination of a dream that had sustained me and millions of my countrymen and women for decades. It was a dream of a South Africa free of racial oppression, a country where every person would have the right to vote and be counted equally.

But the road to that day was not smooth. There were times when the negotiations seemed to be on the brink of collapse, when violence threatened to tear the country apart. I recall the assassination of Chris Hani in April 1993, a blow that nearly pushed the country over the edge. Yet his death also galvanised the nation, and the leadership of the ANC and the government came together to keep the peace.

In the days leading up to the election, I visited various parts of the country, urging people to vote peacefully. I was deeply moved by the sight of long queues of people, many of them elderly, who had waited their whole lives for this moment. They stood for hours in the sun, not in frustration, but in joy. When I cast my own vote in Inanda, I felt a sense of accomplishment that I cannot fully describe. It was as if the whole of South Africa was reborn that day.
sources.context: Mandela's memoir, published in 1994, provides a first-hand account of the negotiations and the election. He highlights the role of compromise and leadership in overcoming crises, such as the assassination of Chris Hani and the rise of right-wing and Inkatha violence. The memoir reflects on the personal and collective significance of the election, emphasising the peaceful transition and the beginning of a new era for South Africa.

expected_answer_points: Source A shows that leaders from different backgrounds came together to negotiate, indicating a compromise.

sources.label: Source A
sources.title: Address to the United Nations General Assembly
sources.author: Mikhail Gorbachev
sources.publication: United Nations General Assembly, New York
sources.content: Excerpt: 'Today, the world is at a turning point. The use or threat of force no longer can be an instrument of foreign policy. The principle of freedom of choice is universal. It is a principle without exceptions. We are not abandoning our convictions, our party, our values, but we do not impose them on others. The de-ideologization of interstate relations has become a demand of the new era. The use of force is a thing of the past. The world is entering an era of peaceful development.'
sources.context: Gorbachev's speech at the UN marked a significant shift in Soviet foreign policy. It announced unilateral reductions in Soviet armed forces and emphasized the primacy of international law and the freedom of choice for all nations. This speech signaled the end of the Brezhnev Doctrine, which had justified Soviet intervention in Eastern Europe, and was a precursor to the revolutions of 1989.

sources.label: Source B
sources.title: The Fall of the Wall
sources.author: Plot against the Cartoon
sources.content: Description: The cartoon depicts the Berlin Wall being demolished by a crowd of people from both sides. In the foreground, a figure representing the Soviet Union is shown watching, with a speech bubble saying 'The wall is gone, but my influence is fading.' The cartoon uses a split-image format: on the left, the Wall is intact with a red flag; on the right, the Wall is crumbling, and people are embracing. The overall tone is optimistic, celebrating the end of division and Soviet influence in Eastern Europe.
sources.context: This cartoon was published shortly after the fall of the Berlin Wall on 9 November 1989. The event was a direct consequence of Gorbachev's reforms and his refusal to use force to keep communist regimes in power. The cartoon captures the moment when Soviet influence collapsed, leading to the end of the Cold War and the emergence of a new world order.

sources.label: Source C
sources.title: The Collapse of the Soviet Union and the New World Order
sources.author: John Lewis Gaddis
sources.publication: The United States and the End of the Cold War: Implications, Reconsiderations, Provocations
sources.content: Excerpt: 'The end of the Cold War was not a victory for the United States alone, but a triumph for the principles of democracy and human rights. The reforms initiated by Gorbachev, though intended to save the Soviet system, ultimately led to its collapse. In Eastern Europe, the peaceful revolutions of 1989 demonstrated the power of popular resistance, as seen in Poland's Solidarity movement. The consequences for South Africa were profound: the end of superpower rivalry removed the ideological justification for apartheid, which was based on anti-communism, and paved the way for the release of Nelson Mandela and the transition to democracy.'
sources.context: John Lewis Gaddis is a prominent Cold War historian. This excerpt reflects the post-Cold War interpretation that the end of the Cold War had global ramifications, including in South Africa. It highlights the interconnectedness of events and the shift in the international balance of power, which created a new world order where democracy and human rights gained ascendancy.

questions.question: Evaluate the reliability of Source C as a historical account of the end of the Cold War. Consider the author's perspective and the context of its publication.
expected_answer_points: Source C is a secondary source written by a historian, John Lewis Gaddis, in 1992, soon after the events, which may limit long-term perspective
Gaddis is a prominent Cold War historian, but his interpretation may reflect a Western triumphalist view, emphasizing democracy and human rights
The source provides a balanced view by crediting Gorbachev's reforms, not just US victory, but it may underplay other factors like economic strain or internal dissent
It is useful for understanding contemporary interpretations, but cross-referencing with primary sources is needed for reliability
The source's focus on South Africa is a specific interpretation that may be seen as oversimplifying complex internal dynamics

questions.question: Compare the perspectives of Source A and Source B on the end of the Cold War. How does each source view the role of the Soviet Union?
expected_answer_points: Source A presents Gorbachev as a proactive reformer, voluntarily renouncing force and embracing freedom of choice, suggesting a positive role for the USSR in ending the Cold War
Source B depicts the Soviet Union as a passive observer, watching its influence fade, implying the USSR was overtaken by events rather than leading them
Both sources agree that the Cold War ended, but they differ on the agency: Source A credits Soviet leadership, while Source B emphasizes popular movements and Soviet decline
Source A is an official speech, aiming to project a positive image, while Source B is a cartoon, using satire to comment on Soviet weakness
Together, they show multiple perspectives: one from within the Soviet leadership, one from outside observers

questions.question: Using all three sources and your own knowledge, discuss the extent to which Gorbachev's reforms were responsible for the end of the Cold War. In your answer, consider other factors such as popular resistance and economic problems.
expected_answer_points: Source A shows Gorbachev's 'new thinking' and reforms (perestroika and glasnost) as key in changing Soviet foreign policy, renouncing force and allowing freedom of choice
Source B highlights the role of popular movements, like the fall of the Berlin Wall, which were enabled by Gorbachev's non-intervention but were not directly caused by him
Source C credits Gorbachev's reforms for leading to the collapse, but also emphasizes the 'peaceful revolutions' and Solidarity in Poland, suggesting a combination of factors
Other factors: economic stagnation in the USSR, the arms race, the role of the US, and the internal contradictions of the Soviet system
Evaluation: Gorbachev's reforms were a necessary but not sufficient condition; they created space for popular resistance, but the collapse was also due to systemic failures
A balanced conclusion: Gorbachev's reforms were pivotal in de-escalating the Cold War, but the end was a result of multiple forces, including popular movements and economic decline

methodology_question.title: Methodology Question
methodology_question.topic: The Truth and Reconciliation Commission as a historical enquiry: testimony, amnesty, reconciliation, usefulness and limitations of evidence
methodology_question.task:
Design a detailed lesson plan for a Grade 12 History class (FET phase) on the topic 'The Truth and Reconciliation Commission as a historical enquiry: testimony, amnesty, reconciliation, usefulness and limitations of evidence'. The lesson should be 60 minutes long and align with the CAPS curriculum for History Grade 12. Your lesson plan must demonstrate your pedagogical skills, not just historical knowledge. You are required to:

- Clearly state the lesson aims and learning outcomes (what students should know and be able to do by the end of the lesson).
- Provide a step-by-step breakdown of the lesson (Introduction, Main Activity, Conclusion) with time allocations for each phase.
- Incorporate at least one primary source (e.g., a TRC testimony excerpt, an amnesty hearing transcript, or a reconciliation statement) and one secondary source (e.g., a historian's analysis or a news article) as part of the lesson resources. Explain how you would use these sources to develop students' historical enquiry skills.
- Include specific historical skills that the lesson will develop (e.g., source analysis, critical thinking, perspective-taking, evaluating evidence, understanding cause and consequence).
- Describe classroom management strategies to ensure all learners are engaged, including differentiation for diverse learning needs (e.g., English language learners, learners with reading difficulties, gifted learners).
- List all resources and materials needed (e.g., handouts, digital tools, whiteboard, etc.).
- Include a brief rationale explaining how your lesson aligns with CAPS requirements and promotes historical enquiry.

Write your lesson plan in a clear, structured format, suitable for submission to a mentor teacher or school department head.
requirements: Lesson steps for teacher and learner

Lesson Steps.3 marks: Clear, detailed steps with logical progression, realistic timing, and clear teacher and learner activities.
Lesson Steps.2 marks: Adequate steps but lacks detail or some timing/activity clarity.

Resources.3 marks: Varied, appropriate resources identified (including at least one primary and one secondary source) with clear explanation of their use.
Resources.2 marks: Some resources mentioned, but not fully explained or only one type of source.

Aim & Outcomes.3 marks: Clear, measurable learning outcomes that align with CAPS and historical enquiry.
Aim & Outcomes.2 marks: Outcomes present but vague or not fully measurable.

Historical Skills.3 marks: Multiple historical skills integrated effectively with explicit teaching strategies.
Historical Skills.2 marks: Some skills mentioned but not fully integrated.

Classroom Management.3 marks: Detailed strategies for diverse learners, including differentiation, engagement, and behaviour management.

CAPS Alignment & Rationale.3 marks: Clear explanation of alignment with CAPS and promotion of historical enquiry.
CAPS Alignment & Rationale.2 marks: Some reference to CAPS but not fully explained.

Overall Clarity & Professionalism.3 marks: Well-organized, professional, and ready for implementation.

essay_question.title: Essay Question
essay_question.topic: To what extent did Gorbachev's reforms and events in Eastern Europe contribute to the end of the Cold War and accelerate political change in South Africa?
essay_question.question: Evaluate the extent to which Gorbachev's reforms (glasnost and perestroika) and the events in Eastern Europe in 1989 contributed to the end of the Cold War and accelerated political change in South Africa. Support your argument with relevant historical evidence.
essay_question.context: The late 1980s witnessed transformative changes globally. In the Soviet Union, Mikhail Gorbachev introduced policies of glasnost (openness) and perestroika (restructuring), which had profound effects on Soviet foreign policy and Eastern Europe. Simultaneously, events such as the fall of the Berlin Wall and the revolutions of 1989 reshaped the international order. In Southern Africa, these developments occurred alongside internal pressures against apartheid. This question invites you to analyse the interconnectedness of these global and regional developments.

Die Nasionale Kurrikulumverklaring Graad R-12 is ’n beleidsverklaring met betrekking tot onderrig en leer in Suid-
Afrikaanse skole en is in die volgende dokumente vervat:

(a) Kurrikulum- en assesseringsbeleidsverklarings vir alle vakke in hierdie dokument opgeneem;

(b) Nasionale beleid met betrekking tot die program-en bevorderingsvereistes van die Nasionale
 Kurrikulumverklaring Graad R-12; en

(c) Nasionale Protokol vir Assessering Graad R-12.

MEV ANGIE MOTSHEKGA, LP
MINISTER VAN BASIESE ONDERWYS
